articles.text: COVID cases have continued to decrease in Alameda County since the end of the year spike spurred by the Omicron variant. Hospitalizations and deaths from the COVID virus, which lag behind case counts, show signs of having peaked as well. At the end of 2020 cases started to rise in November and did not recede to pre-spike levels until March 2021. Dr. George Rutherford, UCSF Professor of Epidemiology explained what was different this time around. “[Omicron] is much more transmissible, so the timeline is sped up. To use a forest fire analogy, [fire quickly] burns up the dry wood,” said Rutherford in December 2021. Here, Omicron is the fire and the dry wood are those that are susceptible to infection due to being unvaccinated, or due to frequent human contact. The peak daily cases during the end of 2020 was 1,260 cases in Alameda County on January 4. Daily Cases On January 4, 2022, exactly one year after the previous year’s peak, COVID cases peaked in Alameda County at 5990. Data in the last seven days is unreliable and subject to change, so the most recent day of more complete data is January 31, when 1,470 cases were reported in the County. An interesting pattern in the case counts is that Sundays regularly have the lowest case counts and Mondays the high case counts, at least in Alameda County. A likely source of this pattern is labs having reporting delays over the weekend, and catching up with processing cases at the start of the work week.

articles.text: In preparation for African American History Month this year, I read Until I Am Free: Fannie Lou Hamer’s Enduring Message To America by Keisha N. Blane. Hamer’s story is integral to the history of the struggle for Black voting rights, women’s empowerment, economic rights and human rights. Born in Webster County, Mississippi, in 1917, Fannie Lou was the youngest of 20 children, the granddaughter of enslaved people, and a sharecropper for much of her life who became a trailblazing activist and organizer. Her best-known words are, “We have a long fight and this fight is not mine alone. But you are not free whether you are white or black, until I am free.” I find it helpful to reflect on Hamer’s life through the lens of the Exodus, particularly Exodus 5: 1-22, the story of Moses’ first attempt to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. After meeting his brother in the desert at God’s Mountain and gathering the leaders of the people in order to gain their trust and share God’s vision of liberation with them, Moses and Aaron go to Pharoah with a very clear command from the Lord: Let my people go so that they can hold a festival for me in the desert. articles.text: Part 1 in a series Do you have a favorite tree or group of trees in Piedmont? How about the grove of European white birch trees growing in the Hall Fenway, the lovely footpath that links Wildwood Avenue to Crocker Avenue near Crocker Park? This unique display features 11 over-arching mature trees growing along the route of a historic rail line that ran through Piedmont. These birches (betula pendula), were designated as Heritage Trees in 2021 upon nomination by Peter and Alicia Fishel. Native to Europe and parts of Asia, these beautiful ornamental trees feature silvery-white bark that becomes marked with irregular black patches as the trees age. Deciduous leaves hang from gracefully pendant thin branches. Varieties including weeping and cutleaf, among others. European white birches have fruiting catkins that ripen and disperse tiny winged seeds into the wind to spread far and wide. These trees are typically planted in groups, as they are in the Hall Fenway. Over the next few weeks, the Piedmont Post will feature a brief article and photo of a Heritage Tree. Other Heritage Trees include a row of seven tall coast redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens), at Linda Beach Field that create an architectural backdrop to the playfield. They were nominated by John Ware with his daughter Sophie, and Betsy Goodman, a member of the Park Commission. Other examples are the grove of Eastern Redbuds at the west end of Piedmont Park off Wildwood, nominated by Lisa Kieraldo; the reclining Coast Live Oak in Piedmont Park, nominated European white birches in the Hall Fenway Photo by Brian Mahany by Will, Finn, and Max Brumfiel; the four evergreen Dogwoods that frame the City Hall entrance, nominated by Bobbe Stehr and Mark Enea; a group of ten Highland Poplars behind Exedra Plaza, nominated by Jim Horner; and a row of seven Dawn Redwoods growing in the former quarry at Dracena Park, nominated by Lyle Gordon. The public is encouraged to seek out these trees to appreciate their beauty, history, and significance. By learning more about the trees that comprise Piedmont’s urban forest, the Park Commission hopes to inspire everyone to seek out special trees in our community and encourage nominations for 2022 Heritage Trees. Submitted nominations will be evaluated on their aesthetic, educational, or historical merits. Nominations are welcome from anyone in the community and trees must be on public property, such as parks, streets, and medians. After vetting by Public Works department arborists, qualifying trees will be forwarded to the Park Commission for review and selection. Nominations are due by March 18 with the winners selected at the Park Commission meeting on April 6. This year’s selections will be announced at the Arbor Day festivities on April 28. Forms are available on the City’s website on its Heritage Tree page at https://www. piedmont.ca.gov/cms/One.aspx? portalId=13659823&pageId= 17970894. There, you can also view an interactive map of the existing Heritage Trees which includes photos of the trees, descriptions, locations, and names of the nominating parties. For more information, please contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or 510-420-3064. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Over the past two years, dozens of people have asked how COVID has impacted Mulberry’s, and what has been the hardest. Almost everyone is surprised by my answer. Sure, the initial scramble for toilet paper, flour and other oddly hoarded staples in the spring of 2020 was hectic. Of course we’ve been desperately worried about the physical and mental health of our team members as they’ve slogged through weeks and months and years of working all day in masks, doing their best to avoid getting infected at work and at home, and weathering the less-than-supportive comments of a customer base with increasingly frazzled nerves. And yeah, managing the ever-changing regulations and inspections required by the CDC, the state of CA, and Alameda County has been exhausting. Yet, with all of that, the most difficult and frustrating problem has been one that predated COVID but has amped up considerably this past year: shoplifting. There have always been shoplifters at Mulberry’s. While it stings every single time – why do they miss the fact that they’re stealing from people? – we’ve always considered it part of the territory. Since 2007, Chad has devoted several hours a week to meeting with young people and their parents, sometimes accompanied by PUSD officials or Piedmont Police Department personnel, to explain to them something that shouldn’t require an explanation: why shoplifting is wrong. In the past year, though, the amount of time he’s devoted to this grim task has skyrocketed. In just the past two months he has dealt with dozens of incidents. Here’s what happens when young shoplifters are caught. Inevitably, they deny that they were taking anything. When we point out that a Mulberry’s employee saw them steal, and that it’s on camera, they often pivot to an excuse/argument that they meant to pay, they just forgot, or had to run outside to get money, or needed to tell a friend something right away and planned to return to the register. Also without exception, they always claim that it is the first time anything like this happened. Generally, we take their name and let them know there will be a call home that night. We also encourage them to tell their parents what happened. During that call, Chad asks the parents to come into the store for a meeting with their child. It’s always better when the shoplifter has already broken the news, but only about half of the kids actually fess up. It’s also better when the parents do not suggest that they, too, think that their child probably got confused or distracted and really, really meant to pay. Regardless of their reaction, he has them come in. During the meeting he usually shows the camera footage. Especially if the shoplifter or his/ her parents are leaning toward the “just got distracted” defense. These meetings are not pleasant. Plenty of kids cry, and some parents do as well. Chad yells. Loudly. He explains how serious shoplifting is, and what might happen if you happened to ‘forget’ to pay for an iPhone at the Apple Store or ‘were just messing around’ and end up talking to a security guard at Target with a bunch of surplus merchandise in your backpack. He appeals to the parents to highlight the fact that most small business owners don’t look like Chad, and don’t share his privilege of a lifetime of feeling like the authorities are on his side. The typical owner of a little store like Mulberry’s is a recent immigrant, working a hundred hours a week and barely scraping by. It’s a brutal business and profit margins are miniscule, and many owners don’t feel like they can count on the police. Parents, we are begging you to talk to your kids about how to avoid ever being in one of those meetings. Help them understand that when they steal from Mulberry’s, they’re stealing from families who live in their town and whose kids go to their school. Tell them that shoplifting makes prices higher for everyone. Explain how demoralizing it is to the Mulberry’s employees, who generally don’t live in Piedmont-like neighborhoods, to see kids with a ton of privilege take exactly what they want – and get away with it. Scare them a little bit and let them know there are consequences for bad choices. We need your help! Mulberry’s loves Piedmont’s kids, and we want to get back to making the store an exciting, fun, welcoming place for Piedmonters of all ages.

articles.text: As California begins to enter the warmer months, many Piedmonters resume gardening. Water-wise gardening is not only useful in the local climate, but also crucial to maintaining a drought-tolerant garden year round. Also known as smart gardening, water-wise gardening uses landscaping techniques to help conserve water while maintaining a beautiful yard. Some common tactics for a water-wise garden include rainwater harvesting, utilizing low-water plants, and maintaining healthy soils with compost and mulch. Focusing on healthy soils, compost and mulch can be utilized for different purposes when maintaining a water-wise garden. Both compost and mulch use can help to reduce the amount of water required by a garden, and it’s important to know the right uses for each. Since soils are a collection of mineral particles of different sizes, large particles allow water to pass through rapidly, while small particles allow the water to penetrate the soil much more slowly. One solution to both large and small particles is adding organic matter (compost and mulch) to improve the texture and water-holding capacity of the soil. When applied in a 3” layer at the least, organic mulch can cut water needs by blocking weeds and reducing evaporation. In addition to retaining moisture, organic mulches also increase the humidity level around plants, feed your soils, and insulate plants from heat and cold. Although there are many varieties of mulch, East Bay Municipal Utility District recommends organic, weedfree, well-composted mulch with a fine to medium texture. Other aspects to consider when selecting a mulch include the type of plants in your garden and the plants heat preferences, the type of soil your garden already has, and expected weather conditions and our local bay area climate. For purposes of moisture retention, organic matter in the form of compost will improve the texture and water-holding capacity of the soil. For amending soil with compost, working a 4” to 8” layer of compost into the soil provides added benefits when establishing new garden beds or transitioning your lawn into a garden. Topdressing, or spreading a half to two-inch layer of compost on top of the soil once or twice a year, is beneficial to existing gardens. Incorporating at least half an inch to an inch of compost in both the spring and fall seasons can also increase plant growth, reduce the need for chemical fertilizers, and improve soil structure through the addition of beneficial bacteria and fungi. Not all soil and compost are created equally. Piedmonters should generally avoid wood chips, large pieces of bark mulch, and synthetic materials based on the climate of the local area. Similarly, it’s best to avoid weed cloths, plastic, and other weed barriers that prevent the natural cycle of nutrients through soils, which can kill the living organisms in your soil. Fortunately, Piedmonters can obtain free organic matter through various giveaways held throughout the year, including this Saturday, February 12, from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. at the City’s Corporation Yard. Learn more about this Saturday’s giveaway and future events at: (https:// w w w.ci.piedmont.ca.us/services_ _ _departments/public_ works/recycling_organic_waste_ garbage/s_b_1383). articles.text: Piedmont resident Mina Fedor, 13, has been named a top 5 honoree for Time Kid of the Year for her work as an Asian American Pacific Islander (AAPI) activist. Fedor will be recognized along Mina Fedor speaks to a crowd at a rally in Berkeley in March 2021. with the other honorees on the Kid of the Year television special, hosted by Trevor Noah on Nickelodeon tonight, February 9. The second annual Kid of the Year honor recognizes young leaders who have made contributions in a range of fields, including social justice, science, and education. The honor is presented by Nickelodeon in partnership with Time Magazine, following a nationwide search that included thousands of youth. “I was really surprised when I received the email. My family and I were taken aback,” Fedor admitted. “I actually don’t even know who submitted me.” At age 12 Fedor organized a rally at the Berkeley Marina on March 28, 2021 to raise awareness of AAPI hate. Over 1,200 community members attended the rally. Fedor, who is of Korean and Slovakian descent, said she has seen hate against the Asian community even when walking near home with a family member. “I was aware of attacks on the Asian community. As last year progressed, I learned more about AAPI history and wanted to educate myself,” Fedor said. “I wasn’t expecting to hold a large rally at first. [My] friends and I had the intention of hanging signs over a highway that I drive under every day I go to school.” Fedor and her peers made signs that read “I Am Not a Virus,” and “Stop Asian Hate,” while leading a crowd on a march over a pedestrian bridge. Fedor recalls cars honking in support. She expected a crowd would show up in support at the Berkeley Marina but never expected it to grow to over 1000 people. Fedor co-founded the activist group AAPI Youth Rising, comprised of herself and other middle schoolers. They have worked toward a goal of passing state Photo by Jose Carlos Fajardo Mina Fedor legislation that would make the teaching of ethnic studies mandatory in public high schools. That law passed in October 2021. “It’s extremely important to know about other’s stories, and your own. That’s a big part about growing up as an American citizen,” she said. “Representation means everything. When you learn stories similar to yours, or about people who look like you, you feel like your experiences are more valid.” Each of the eight honorees will receive a cash prize and the opportunity to serve as a reporter for Time for Kids, a subsidiary of Time Magazine. Viewers can watch the premiere on the Nickelodeon channel tonight, February 9, at 4:30 p.m.

The second annual Kid of the Year honor recognizes young leaders who have made contributions in a range of fields, including social justice, science, and education. Fedor recalls cars honking in support. She expected a crowd would show up in support at the Berkeley Marina but never expected it to grow to over 1000 people. Fedor co-founded the activist group AAPI Youth Rising, comprised of herself and other middle schoolers. That law passed in October 2021. “It’s extremely important to know about other’s stories, and your own. That’s a big part about growing up as an American citizen,” she said. “Representation means everything. articles.text: A Thousand Splendid Suns chosen for 2022 Piedmont High School has announced the official launch of Readmont 2022, Piedmont’s annual community read project now in its 12th year. All Piedmonters are encouraged to read A Thousand Splendid Suns by Khaled Hosseini. The book was published in 2007 and chronicles the story of two generations of women, Mariam and Laila, living in Kabul. The story not only portrays the bonds of family and friendship and the endurance of women during Taliban control, but also gives readers a look into the backdrop of the recent history of Afghanistan. We chose this book for its beautiful story of love in an unforgiving time and as a way for our community to discuss the recent events in Afghanistan and the increase of Afghan refugees to the Bay area. The book is appropriate for readers age 14 and older. To encourage younger readers to learn about the topic, the school is also promoting two books appropriate for 6-10 year olds, I am Malala, and Malala - my story for standing up for Girls’ Rights. Books are available for check out at all Piedmont school libraries (high school, middle school, and three elementary schools). The books are funded through a grant from the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee (PADC). A Great Good Place for Books in Montclair is offering a 20% discount on this title. The hope is that this common reading experience will forge positive connections among students, staff, parents and community members, and encourage reading as a medium of collaboration. English department chairperson Beth Black and high school librarian Kathryn Levenson will facilitate student discussions during the week of April 19, and host guest speakers on the topic the evening of April 21. All events are open to the community. More information will follow regarding the community events. If you have questions, contact Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us, 510-594-2781, or Beth Black at bblack@piedmont.k12.ca.us.

articles.text: At the January 26 School Board meeting Superintendent Randy Booker presented the board with a report on enrollment capacity throughout the district. The board requested that a survey be conducted to help determine the amount of inter-district transfers that may be accepted for next year. The study found that in grades 1-5 there will be 56 seats available at Beach, 42 at Havens and 35 at Wildwood if the district is at maximum capacity. At the middle school there are an estimated 186 open seats, 75 at Piedmont High and 27 at Millennium High. These numbers do not take into account projected gains and losses after the school year starts, due to students transferring in or out. For example, during a non-pandemic year Piedmont High averages a decrease of roughly ten 9th graders in the middle of the year. Using current numbers for next year, the 9th grade class could add 27 more students. Therefore, considering the midyear exits of 10 students, the district estimates a total of 37 more students that could possibly be added next year before reaching capacity. The current collective bargaining between the district and teachers union limits staffing to student ratio at 1:28 or less. The California Department of Education provides additional funding to districts with a ratio under 1:24 at the K-3 levels. The district plans to limit grades 1-3 to 24 students per class, and the capacity for 4-5 graders is 26 instead of the maximum 28 due to PEF funding. Grades 6-12 have a capacity of 1:28 teacher to staff ratio and Millennium High has a maximum ratio at 1:20. Piedmont School District receives around $9,700 per student from state and federal funds. For every 28 students added, the school district adds approximately one and half fulltime teacher salary. The student increase gives the district around $126,100 and costs the district roughly $124,000 in salary. Booker anticipates competition between Alameda County schools for inter-district transfers. “Absolutely, 100% yes [there will be competition]. Every district in Alameda County is looking for students, except for Dublin,” he said. articles.text: The Piedmont School Board approved a first reading of a proposed new class, Film as Literature, to be taught by Mercedes Foster. The first reading serves as an opportunity for Board members to review and discuss the content of the course proposal before it is added to the high school curriculum. It will be a new elective course within the English Department for students in grades 11 and 12. Students will be instructed on how to use literary terminology and analytical techniques learned in their prerequisite English classes to explore films with cultural or societal merit. Students will watch and critically analyze these films, as well as screenwriting choices, sound design, and directional design. “Although the Piedmont High School humanities courses traditionally have included the occasional film or film clip as part of the curriculum, the material is generally used to supplement other material. Rarely is film or video explicitly examined as a piece of art, let alone examined critically as a product of our culture. Exploring film takes time that is not available in the college preparatory English classes,” Foster explained in her course proposal. “We want this course to include relevant experiences that invite fresh conversations, and address the interests and concerns of the students,” Foster said. Students will have the opportunity to use what they learn in the course to produce their own films through online editing software. In addition, the new STEAM building includes a sound booth editing room that will allow students to mix, record or edit overlay audio. Foster noted that many Bay Area schools have a Digital Media class built into their curriculum, notably at Oakland Tech and Palo Alto, or a Film and Media Arts Department like the one at South Torrance High. The School Board unanimously approved the first reading of the course. A second reading will determine whether or not the course will be made available, although School Board President Cory Smegal noted that it will likely get approved. “That’s the most likely thing to happen, unless we hear [opposition] from the public. But the only thing I think we’d hear is that they would really like to take this class,” she said.

articles.text: Piedmont Adult School is in full swing, and is offering new courses on climate change and parenting. Classes in progress can still be joined and many have yet to commence. Climate Change 101 Are you concerned about climate change and looking for a way to become better informed? Climate Change 101, a course “by a non-scientist for non-scientists,” is being offered by Piedmont Adult School on March 2 and 3. This two-evening course covers the causes and impacts of climate change and provides students with the knowledge required to make informed decisions. Students will receive useful handouts as well as references for further study. Climate Change 101 is taught by James Stehr, a Piedmont High School graduate in 1960. Stehr graduated with honors from UC Berkeley and went on to a career in architecture. Upon retirement, he decided to pursue his interest in the sciences, and became a project leader for Al Gore’s Climate Reality Project. A man of many interests, Stehr also holds a certificate in financial planning. He will also teach a course at the Adult School in March called Tools and Techniques for Navigating Retirement. Mindful Positive Parenting Austin Lambe returns to teach his popular course, Mindful Positive Parenting starting on March 8. The six-week course is designed to provide parents with a space to share concerns and learn new parenting strategies. The class will focus on behavior challenges that are commonly faced by parents: screen time, work refusal, respectful communications, homework, and friendships. The first four classes will explain the principles of behavior and the last four will be devoted to generating interventions and strategies that can be implemented immediately at home. Lambe lives in Oakland but hails originally from Ireland. He is married and a parent of two teenagers. He is a board certified behavior analyst and he works as the Behavior Analyst for Piedmont School District. He has spent his career coaching students, teachers and parents on challenging behaviors in a variety of settings. Lambe has a background in Clinical Psychology and has a passion for helping others to solve behavior puzzles. For more information and to sign up, visit Piedmontadultschool.org. Classes are open to all adults age 18 and over. Piedmont Adult School offers in-person as well as online classes. In-person classes will be held at Piedmont High School and will follow Piedmont School District COVID-19 guidelines. The Piedmont Adult School office is located at 760 Magnolia Avenue. For information call (510) 594-2655, or e-mail: piedmontadultschool@piedmont. k12.ca.us.

articles.text: How can we encourage our children to dream? For many of our kids, the last two years have been an experience in limiting – limiting which activities we can do and when, limiting our social engagements, and limiting where we travel or visit. But our kids are at the beginning of their journey. We want them thinking and dreaming as big as the sea and as wide as the sky. The fastest gateway to dreaming big is encouraging imagination. Imagination gives kids permission to see past what is directly in front of them and believe in possibility. Many kids naturally have a huge imagination that are equal parts expansive and detailed. We as parents have the power to encourage their imagination or shut it down. In Improvisation, actors are trained to use the concept of “Yes, and…” to grow a scene or story instead of shrinking it. We call it “accepting an offer” when one actor says something and the other person builds on the idea. For example, Actor 1 says, “I love visiting the zoo with you.” Actor 2 has a choice, she can say, “This isn’t the zoo, it’s an ice cream parlor,” thus limiting the scope of the scene or she can say “Yes, the lions are looking particularly hungry today, should we bring them some ice cream?” And we are off to the races! All of a sudden, we have a really interesting story to tell about two people at a zoo who are going to make an ice cream parlor in a lion’s den. How does this concept apply to parenting? Well, the next time your child starts to talk about an imaginary friend or a crazy Cultivate the power of imagination in your child. dream they had or a story they are making up in their mind, think of “Yes, and..” to encourage them to keep using that powerful imagination! Other ways to encourage that kind of dreaming are all forms of expressive arts including drawing, painting, dancing and singing. Exposing children to great stories through books, movies and theatre is also a terrific stimulation for the mind. As we climb slowly out of Pandemic living, let’s give our kids the chance to dream as big and as wild as they can. With imagination, they have the power to shape the world in ways that we have never fathomed and that gives me hope for the future. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: Staff Photos Soccer coach Dan Chubbock has two matches left in the season before the NCS playoffs. Hitting something of a dry spell, the girls’ soccer team couldn’t produce any scoring in its most recent pair of gams, losing 1-0 to rival Bishop O’Dowd on Monday, February 7 at home, and being held scoreless in a 0-0 draw with San Leandro at Burrell Field on Thursday, February 3. The results effectively assured Berkeley the league championship among teams in the WACC Foothill Division. “We just didn’t create enough. We need to find a way to open up gaps and create chances,” said coach Dan Chubbock. “We’re not going to change the system this late in the season. We just need to open the gaps and find that end product. The Highlanders have struggled with creating goals since January 21 when they defeated Arroyo 4-1. Piedmont hasn’t scored more than one goal per game in the last six matches, and is scoreless in its last three. “We just haven’t scored enough goals. We don’t have a natural center forward. We have a lot of good players, we move the ball around really well, we just don’t quite create the chances and find that finishing touch,” said Chubbock. Piedmont has two league matches left, hosting Castro Valley for Senior Night tonight, Wednesday, February 9 at Witter Field, and the season-finale at league champion Berkeley on Friday, February 11. North Coast Section playoffs begin on Tuesday and Wednesday, February 15-16. If the Highlanders win the last two home games of the season, they may be enough to earn a top 8 NCS seed, with the possibility of at least one playoff game at Witter Field. 1-0 loss to Bishop O’Dowd Bishop O’Dowd’s goal came in the 31st minute on a fortunate bounce after a corner kick. In the buildup, the cross from the corner went over a leaping O’Dowd forward and fell at the feet of BOD captain Katie Senn for the open shot. Earlier in the 19th minute, Piedmont goalkeeper Morgan Hunt made a big save in a 1-on-1 situation. She came up big again in the 71st minute with another dramatic save. In the second half, the Highlanders came out on the front foot but couldn’t find the finishing touch. Tucker Donahue had a shot trail high in the 42nd, Emily Fitzgerald also had a shot go high in the 57th after Zoe Wolfers played a nice pass in traffic to her. In the late minutes, Fitzgerald had a shot skip wide of the far post after working down the right wing. Cameron Lorin had a shot saved in the 78th which gave PHS a corner kick. Piedmont brought forward Hunt, but the ball in was cleared out. 1-0 tie with San Leandro Against San Leandro, it was a similar story of not finding the finishing touch in the final third of the field. In the first half, Piedmont had five shots on target and seven total shots taken, but a monumental save by the Pirates’ keeper in the 38th minute, diving to her left, deflected a shot from Donahue for what likely would have been the winning goal. In the second half, Piedmont had fewer shots on target. Donahue had a shot on target from distance in the 61st minute and Fitzgerald had a shot ring off the crossbar in the 68th. articles.text: Piedmont residents Stacey Isaacs and Chuck Wolf have a lot to be thankful for this Valentine’s Day. They will be celebrating almost four years of marriage, but the college sweethearts’ love story begins in 1984. The couple met 30 years ago at UCLA where he was studying history and she was studying communications, both joined Greek Societies and met at a fraternity party. Chuck recalled that he knew Stacey would be the woman he’d marry when he first saw her. “We dated in college, and we were madly in love,” he said. “We fell in love while we were growing up,” Stacey added. But after graduating in 1985, Chuck worked with the military and was transferred to the East Coast. He traveled the world and spent almost a decade working in Virginia and Washington, D.C. Meanwhile Stacey lived and worked in the Bay Area as a business executive with Clorox, Ghiradelli and Diamond Foods, eventually becoming a Realtor with Highland Partners in Piedmont. It wasn’t until a little over three years ago, when Chuck returned to the Bay Area for work, that the couple reconnected and rekindled the love they shared in college. When Chuck settled in Palo Alto, he reached out to Stacey asking her to join him for a cup of coffee. Chuck admitted that he had to press Stacey to meet him after she rescheduled a few times. “I told her to just give me half an hour,” he said. Both acknowledged that at that first “re-meeting” it was as if no time had passed. Since then, the two have enjoyed skiing in Tahoe, camping trips to Lake Shasta, and spending time with their nowblended family. Stacey has lived in Piedmont for 11 years, and after reconnecting, Chuck moved to town, too. The couple even exchanged nuptials in Piedmont. “He sailed his boat from the East Coast to Texas and then shipped the boat to Piedmont. And he’s been here with me ever since,” she said. Valentine’s Day holds special significance for the couple as a time to reflect on their journey to reconnecting and simply enjoying each other’s company. “I think Valentine’s Day is more than just the romance of that day. It’s more of a celebration of your entire life together – a nice mark on the calendar that you should be thankful for the other,” Chuck said. This year, the couple will plan to have an at-home dinner together with teenage son William. Stacey’s favorite Valentine’s Day gift to receive from Chuck are simple and sweet cards. “I would love to get her a dozen roses...but I’m allergic,” he said with a laugh. articles.text: Patty and Carter Dunlap in December. Carter sports one of his festive outfits, a matching polyester sport coat and tie. In 2000, Carter Dunlap and Patty Fleshman were set up by a mutual friend in a matchmaking plot. Their cupid, Mary MacRae, invited both of them to her house, but Patty could not make it. Unperturbed by the missed connection, Carter invited her for drinks in San Francisco that weekend. The targets of cupid’s arrow turned out to make for a classic match. Astrology charts say their union is destined for success. Patty is a Taurus and Carter is a Capricorn, both signs of the earth, with excellent compatibility. With two children each, they were married in May 2003 creating a blended family. Carter’s kids, Wes and Carmel and Patty’s daughter and son, Taylor and Trevor, soon became fast friends and their Piedmont home a place of love and community. This year marks 22 years since they first met, making this Valentine’s Day a special occasion. “We are going to have to step it up this year for Valentine’s Day,” Carter said. “We are still working through this very cute book: The Best Places to Kiss in Northern California, so we might look through that,” added Patty. Their chemistry is obvious upon first sight of the couple. “Most people that know us consider us to be hopelessly romantic, in an endearing but kind of goofy way. Patty has nicknames for me and vice versa. We exhibit public displays of affection,” confirmed Carter. “Yes, we kiss in public,” Patty noted. When asked what quirks of their spouse they particularly enjoy, Patty said, “Almost every day Amazon comes to our house with something new. My husband is a shopper,” she said with a smile. Carter quickly countered with one of his favorite mannerisms of Patty, “When my wife is being silly she combines the behavior of Lucy with Desi Arnaz, she dances around like Lucy but with Ricky’s accent,” Carter said. When they married, Carter promised Patty they would visit a new country every year. For their 15th anniversary in 2018 they went to Paris, for a romantic getaway that was particularly memorable. Carter explained the complexity of “rules” to the travel commitment. “There were no points in France because Patty had been to France before, but had not been to Switzerland, and it was the opposite for me,” he said. Now approaching 22 years, 2022 promises to have many new adventures. What is their secret to love everlasting? “For me, Valentine’s Day gives me a chance to celebrate love in all its shapes and forms, it doesn’t always have to be romantic love. It is love you have for your friends and kids and mom. It is a time to put those sentiments first,” said Patty.

articles.text: John and Sue Malick Sue Malick has kept every Valentine’s Day card her husband John has given her – more than 40...and counting. The two met on a blind date in 1972. Sue was an undergraduate at Wheaton College in Massachusetts studying political science and John was a first-year graduate studying architecture at Yale. “I was set up on a blind date by some friends, but he had a family emergency. John was actually the substitute blind date,” Sue said with a laugh. “My friends asked me if I would see him again and I thought if I see him again, that’s it. I won’t be seeing anyone else.” The pair found they had a lot in common from the get-go. Sue admits that, although she majored in political science, her true love was studying architectural art history. “I found what he was studying very compelling,” she said. “My best memories of our courtship was when we were trying to find interesting things to do that were not the ‘sweep-you-off-your-feet moments.’” Sue recalled their third date, when the couple was taking a walk through New Haven. “We were walking around the city, and he was telling me about the architectural style of the buildings. We were both reading the visual arts book ‘Learning to Look’ in college, and John told me to look at the tops of the buildings. The era they were built offered tremendous richness at the top corners. “We both looked up and it was like the world exploded with texture and color,” she said. “To me, that was one of the most eye-opening, wonderful dates.” John remembered one of his favorite dates early on, when he took Sue to East Rock overlooking the city of New Haven. “We have a running joke; we would stand there, overlooking the city, and I’d tell her ‘someday, this will all be yours,’” he said with a laugh. “It’s still a running joke – at the Hoover Dam, the top of Mt. Tam, we look out at the 360-degree view and I say the same thing.” “And that view is really richer than anything you could ever buy,” Sue added. “Seeing the world from that perspective … it did become yours, in that this was a shared experience,” John said. The couple dated for three years before getting married in 1975. Sue and John lived in Portland briefly while he worked for Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, a global architectural and urban planning firm. The couple moved to Piedmont in 1983 for its schools, and laid roots in town raising their three children together. Sue said that her favorite gift on the most romantic of holidays is a hand-written card from John. “I’ve kept every one. They’re funny, they’re romantic, they’re cute, and clever,” she said. “It means the world to me.” “Producing that card is what makes Valentine’s Day unique. It’s not like it’s a weeklong effort. Some years I’m sitting at my desk and think, oh gee, it’s Valentine’s Day, I have ten minutes to make something clever and pithy and meaningful.” “But it’s like if you forced an artist to play Pictionary, he can do something miraculous like that on the fly!” Sue said with a smile. “WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX”* *On all installed jobs

Sue admits that, although she majored in political science, her true love was studying architectural art history. “I found what he was studying very compelling,” she said. “My best memories of our courtship was when we were trying to find interesting things to do that were not the ‘sweep-you-off-your-feet moments.’” Sue recalled their third date, when the couple was taking a walk through New Haven. “We were walking around the city, and he was telling me about the architectural style of the buildings. We were both reading the visual arts book ‘Learning to Look’ in college, and John told me to look at the tops of the buildings. The era they were built offered tremendous richness at the top corners. “We both looked up and it was like the world exploded with texture and color,” she said. “To me, that was one of the most eye-opening, wonderful dates.” John remembered one of his favorite dates early on, when he took Sue to East Rock overlooking the city of New Haven. “We have a running joke; we would stand there, overlooking the city, and I’d tell her ‘someday, this will all be yours,’” he said with a laugh. “It’s still a running joke – at the Hoover Dam, the top of Mt. Tam, we look out at the 360-degree view and I say the same thing.” “And that view is really richer than anything you could ever buy,” Sue added. “Seeing the world from that perspective … it did become yours, in that this was a shared experience,” John said. The couple dated for three years before getting married in 1975. Sue and John lived in Portland briefly while he worked for Skidmore, Owings and Merrill, a global architectural and urban planning firm. The couple moved to Piedmont in 1983 for its schools, and laid roots in town raising their three children together. Sue said that her favorite gift on the most romantic of holidays is a hand-written card from John. “I’ve kept every one. They’re funny, they’re romantic, they’re cute, and clever,” she said. “It means the world to me.” “Producing that card is what makes Valentine’s Day unique. It’s not like it’s a weeklong effort. Some years I’m sitting at my desk and think, oh gee, it’s Valentine’s Day, I have ten minutes to make something clever and pithy and meaningful.” “But it’s like if you forced an artist to play Pictionary, he can do something miraculous like that on the fly!” Sue said with a smile. articles.text: Visit the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art now through March 6 to see Rafael Lozano-Hemmer’s exhibition “Unstable Presence.” Lozano-Hemmer’s exhibit was slated to premiere in Spring 2020, but was delayed due to COVID safety precautions. In describing the work, the artist said the title is meant to be a paradox. “Presence is often associated with existence, continuity in time, or material reality. The ‘unstable’ here refers to interaction, improvisation, and performance. The instability brought by participation is welcome, because it allows constant reinterpretation of the work,” Lozano-Hemmer said. With a degree in chemistry, the artist works primarily with media and technology to create artwork. Many of his works include some aspect of interactivity. “Sometimes I think of media artwork as not so much part of the visual arts, but the performing arts,” he said. “You’ve got a score, but that score gets interpreted by different orchestras in a different way. Sometimes we pretend we’re crystallizing a moment in time, when in fact what the artist wants is for the artwork to have, on the one hand, a decent life, and then an honorable death,” he said. To obtain tickets, visit https:// www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/ rafael-lozano-hemmer-unstable-presence/.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre (Berkeley Rep) will be showing Swept Away, directed by Michael Mayer, now through March 6 at Peet’s Theatre. Tony Award-winning director Mayer returns to Berkeley Rep with this world premiere musical based on the book by John Logan. Music and lyrics for the production are by roots band the Avett Brothers, with choreography by David Neumann. Swept Away takes place off the coast of New Bedford, Massachusetts, where a violent storm sinks a ship leaving four people stranded. Each character faces a reckoning and audiences will see how far they will go to stay alive - and if they can live with the consequences. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony finally gets its season-opening concert After the Berkeley Symphony concert, conductor Joseph Young chatted with the enthusiastic audience. The mood was festive in Zellerbach Hall this past Sunday afternoon. A large and enthusiastic audience cheered the Berkeley Symphony as it embarks on its Golden Jubilee season, exactly two years to the day since its last concert in Zellerbach. The good fortune was to have Joseph Young as conductor. The repertoire was chosen carefully and, as such, could only happen in Berkeley. Considering it as a stream of consciousness concert, it made me wonder: what if James Joyce were a composer or a music director? First he would need to be from Berkeley. He would certainly let his imagination run wild. Music turns on the imagination like a veritable stream of consciousness when one thought becomes many History and the present blend into a panoramic canvas. Then, all of that would be needed to become a word picture. A few words of explanation from the composers Mark Grey and Derek Skye began the concert. The stage and the auditorium were darkened. As the program began, so did the stream of consciousness; somewhat akin to walking in the cosmos unfettered and James Joyce as composer and music director. First came Mark Grey’s Soundscape #1. With the stage darkened and voices of protest emanating as the center of attention, it conjured up a terrifying experience of being an innocent bystander during one of the violent political-social demonstrations near Zellerbach in the ‘60s. The stream of consciousness moved on seamlessly to Morton Gould’s Protest. Not realizing the context of the programming, I was impressed by the Symphony’s brass and woodwind sections. Their resonance was truly impressive. The program moved on seamlessly to Soundscape #2, also by Mark Grey. Once again the feeling of terrible trepidation returned. Perhaps the soft sections should have been played softer, but my thoughts were directed to Sibelius himself. While I did not know this stupendous genius personally, I have been a friend of his granddaughter for many years. The stories she told me about being with grandfather Sibelius became even more vivid. I vowed to be a grandfather like he was. After intermission the concert resumed with Lollapalooza by Berkeley composer John Adams who enjoys enthusiastic popularity. Once again, the stream of consciousness resumed and I was reminded of the great American composer Charles Ives. As an orchestra, the Berkeley Symphony is at the top of its game. It is quite obvious that the conductor, Joseph Young, is an inspiring influence, and it is fortuitous that Berkeley Symphony was able to engage him as their music director in 2019. The orchestra’s most inspiring playing came at the end with Igor Stravinsky’s evocative Firebird suite. Of particular note were beautiful solos played by oboist Bennie Cottone and bassoonist Rufus Olivier. And once again, the stream of consciousness overcame reality. articles.text: Mare Winningham and Alison Lohman in Sharing the Secret. Sharing the Secret, released in 2000, has at its focus teenager Beth Moss (Alison Lohman), who, from all outward appearances, leads a perfect life. She is attractive, popular at school, excels at school and ballet. It’s hard to imagine that she is experiencing anything other than your typical adolescent issues. And yet, we soon discover that she is suffering silently, worried that she is not meeting her family’s expectations and doesn’t feel like she is in control of her life. She is also coping with the conflicting emotions brought about by the recent divorce of her parents – child psychologist Dr. Nina Moss (Mare Winningham), and her dad, John Moss (Tim Matheson). Searching for a way to control her life she turns to the eating disorders bulimia and anorexia, secretly purging after meals and eating far less than she should. Gradually, as a result of this extreme behavior, she becomes symptomatic, beginning with a dizzying misstep in her ballet class, and begging her instructor not to tell her mother. Soon Beth notices that her gums are beginning to bleed. As the story progresses, Beth becomes more and more adept at hiding her symptoms. But one day she passes out in the school hallway. Instead of calling her mother, she asks the school to get in touch with her new stepmother (Mary Crosby), hoping to avoid involving Nina. When her father, John, insists that Beth see the family doctor, he discovers that she is anemic. When he questions her about her diet, she insists that she eats properly and all is well. When Beth returns to school, it is her counselor (Khaditah Karrlem) who confronts her with her suspicions that she is bulimic and tells Beth to discuss this issue with her mother – something Beth has gone to great lengths to avoid, She tells the counselor with conviction that she has no problems. When Beth finally concludes she has no choice, she does speak with her mother, but still denies that anything is wrong. It causes a major conflict between Beth and Nina, who is increasingly concerned, and finds herself in the role as a psychologist first, and mother second. The result is that Beth gets her own psychologist. The film does a fine job of demonstrating the hold that this syndrome can have over young, vulnerable females and how difficult it is to defeat the impulse of denial. Sharing the Secret has been ranked by Disordered Times with its top rating for the portrayal of bulimia and anorexia. It has been praised as one of the best movies made about this deeply disconcerting afflictions, while demonstrating the impact it has on not only the individual but on the entire family. It is a film worthy of analysis and discussion. Sharing the Secret. Directed by Katt Shea. Starring Mare Winningham, Alison Lohman, Tim Matheson. Streaming on Amazon Prime. 2 hrs., Rated PG.

articles.text: No doubt the world of Cormac McCarthy, author of the novel The Road, is bleak and austere. Recall his dark and nihilistic book, No Country for Old Men, which was adapted to the screen by the Coen brothers, garnering four Academy Awards, including Best Picture. This film, made in 2009, is perhaps the most severe of all of McCarthy’s stories and director John Hillcoat follows the novel closely. The film is set during a post-apocalyptic period, one that has caused an ecological disaster, not unlike a nuclear winter. What happened is never made clear. The skies are leaden, a perpetual mist falls, all is grim and gray. A father (Viggo Mortensen) and his son (Kodi Smit-McPhee) are on a road headed to the Pacific Ocean ten years after the catalytic event. Few people have survived the long, torturous decade. Most have starved, been killed or committed suicide. The father and son are faced with overwhelming odds: they are desperate for food and constantly fearful of those they might meet along the way. The fragile patina of civilization has been scraped away revealing the most sinister aspects of the human condition. They hide constantly from predators who will resort to anything to stay alive. Anything. All taboos have been broken. This intersection between order and chaos, between laws and anarchy, intrigue McCarthy, and it’s this that he explores in withering detail in The Road. Know that the post-apocalyptic setting of this film does not resemble Hollywood movies about natural disasters. What is unique about it is that it is unrelentingly stark, with only a glimmer of hope embedded in this harsh tale. The performances of Viggo Mortensen and Kodi SmitMcPhee are impressive. And with the exception of brief backstory on the mother (Charlize Theron), it is the father and son who make the journey. It is their bond of love, their will to survive against all odds, that make for a compelling tale. Some might feel that the story is too forbidding to be enjoyed, but The Road is an antidote to Hollywood’s typical post-apocalyptic storytelling. The Road. Directed by John Hillcoat. Starring Viggo Mortensen, Kodi Smit-McPhee, Charlize Theron and Robert DuVall. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated R. A scene from John Hillcoat’s The Road.

articles.text: Part 37 in a biweekly series One of the most useful ways to form a vision of how we would prefer future development to proceed in our communities is by gathering examples of what we like—and dislike. We can do this by simply being aware of our surrounding built environment, making mental notes and asking the questions: do we like what we see? Do we like the way a neighborhood feels? Do we want to come back to this place? This search for examples should extend as far and wide as we can take it. The world is a big place with many centuries of development. We can still learn from places that were built long ago in places far away just as we can from recent local projects. The “why” we feel the way we do is important as well because no two places are exactly the same. For this reason simply copying examples outright doesn’t work—we are never going to find models that exactly fit our situation, our street, or our city. However if we understand the reasons, the underlying principles of the things and places we like or dislike, we can adapt design solutions accordingly. This is the point where innovation – and hopefully – progress in urban design, architectural design, and landscape design can take place. Why wouldn’t we emulate the successful formula found all over the globe such as in Havana, Cuba, where (real) units above the ground floor provide actual housing, city texture, and security in the sense of “eyes on the street”, not to mention customers for the ground floor commercial.

Below is my sage advice as you begin to approach your project. Prioritize Teamwork: Construction is not linear, and there is no right or wrong way to launch it. If there is a vendor you already trust – whether an architect, designer, landscape architect, or contractor – start there. See A Life by Design on page 32 Ask Questions: Whether for your established home or a new purchase, it cannot be overstated that the time spent interviewing, vetting, and selecting your team should be done with thoughtful intention. When the going gets tough, you want to understand who and how someone will be under high pressure and trust that they will maintain the momentum. Find out how delays are dealt with, preferred methods and frequency of communication, and how scope creep or scope change is handled. Ask how they handle vendors when work quality is below their standards – or yours. Then listen. If you pay attention, you can quickly discern if you’re in the company of a team player or someone operating from ego. Look out for stories that reflect defensiveness. Trust you’ll be in good hands when interacting with someone who has spent time self-reflecting and taking responsibility for their mistakes. Temper Expectations: You may be stepping in with optimism regarding timelines, unaware of how decimated the supply chain remains due to the pandemic. Good vendors are in high demand, and this is true across the board with professionals in all home industries. If you’re planning a remodel in 2023 and desire custom, high-quality work, it’s not too soon to start your search now. articles.text: On February 2 members of the Walking on Wednesdays group stopped for a photo by a classic Victorian home built in 1896. Pictured are our Wednesday Walkers: Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Rob Smith, Dave DeRoche, Priscilla Wanerus, Bob Gustafson, Peter Persoff, Sherry Jacobs, Quincy Dong, Harriette Louie, Jim Kuo, Albert Chen, Aaron Katzel, Pat McMahon, Lilly Guardia-Labor, Pat Keller, Christine Calliste, Maulshree Solanki, Adriene Hamlin, Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Brenda Ferrero, Charlene Louie, Sarah Johnson, Elane Rehr, Kat Lang, Alan Goldhammer, Renee Goldhammer, Phil Witte, Jim Kellogg, John Lenahan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Melba Yee, and Dick Carter. The group was especially pleased to welcome four first-time walkers: Stacy Readal, Nitesh Mehta, Richard Siegel, and Dale Benveniste. Last Wednesday was a cool, breezy morning for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Wednesday Walkers and was windy enough for a kite flyer to test his skills on the grass in Piedmont Park. The pleasant, dry winter weather brought out another large assembly, this time 38 walkers and one K-9 best friend. The walkers enjoy finding Piedmont’s 21 hidden pathways. Gail Lombardi, president of the Piedmont Historical Society, has told us that with Piedmont’s large blocks, these paths have saved countless steps for students going to and from school, and commuters walking to the streetcar lines and bus stops. A primary economic driver of the area before and after the city was incorporated in 1907 has been residential real estate, and people’s ability to get to, around, and through the area has been vital in its development. In 1878 Walter Blair, the first European settler of the area, created a horse-drawn trolley car from the Mountain View cemetery entrance Blair Park along today’s Moraga Avenue, and to the Piedmont Springs Hotel where the Exedra is today. Visitors liked the area and bought land. Frank C. Havens, the area’s most impactful early real estate developer, partnered in 1895 with Francis Marion “Borax” Smith. They formed the “Realty Syndicate” which, among other projects, built the Claremont Hotel and was originally the parent company of the Key System transit company. It operated in Piedmont, Oakland, and the rest of the East Bay as well as San Francisco, and it brought land buyers to the area. Homeowners wanted to be able to easily get to the Key System trains, and pathways were drawn into neighborhood master plans to accommodate them. Many of these paths are still serving Piedmonters and provide fun walks for the Walking on Wednesdays group. The Key System’s No. 12 line went from today’s Jerome and Fairview Avenue down to Grand Avenue and then to downtown Oakland. There are three hidden paths in this part of Piedmont that the walkers chose as their destination for the morning. Off the walkers went down Magnolia Avenue looking for a 246-foot path between the houses at 144 and 200 Magnolia. The parade of walkers got separated briefly as they stopped at the Larmer Court cul-de-sac to regroup. The group continued and found a path that took them down to Palm Drive. It was once Frank Havens’ “Avenue of the Palms” – a grand entrance his Piedmont Park attraction with a hedge maze where Piedmont High’s Witter Field is today. The walkers admired the palms and continued on to where the street becomes Wildwood Avenue. They passed the triangular park with its redwood tree grove and took a right on what is now curiously Nova Drive, not Magnolia Avenue. Three houses layer they came to their second hidden path. This one is 249 feet long and goes up to Fairview Avenue, the street that was once part of the Key System 12 Line. Fairview has upper and lower streets that are separated by a long green space. This was once part of the Key System right-ofway land and the streets are connected by another path. The search for the day’s third hidden path was a little tricky. The walkers went up Fairview to Arbor Drive, then down to the circle where it intersects with Nova Drive and continued up to 112 and 116 Arbor. Between these two homes is 110-foot path with some steep stairs that leads to another cul-de-sac, MacKinnon Place which is connected to Magnolia Avenue. They went down Park View, turned right on Winsor Avenue and left on Wildwood Avenue past Wildwood School and to the lower entrance of Piedmont Park, which now attracts many off-leash dogs and their owners. Rather than take the shorter upper trail, the group took the lower one that runs along Bushy Dell Creek. The creek’s almost constant watering of the trees along its bank has resulted in some huge eucalyptus and redwood trees. A former mineral springs grotto was another point of interest. It was visited by Mark Twain around 1869 when he was on a lecture tour in San Francisco. It had been a morning filled with historical paths, interesting streets, and good conversation with new and old friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at: https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: Nº 48 in a biweekly series There’s no Welcome Wagon in France, commented my friend Ed recently. I was lamenting the myriad ways we’ve felt tripped up by French bureaucracy for the visa or healthcare and muttering about lost applications that had to be resubmitted resulting in duplicates and causing havoc. We’ve dutifully obtained translations into French of birth certificates, bank statements, and IRS 1040s. We’ve pledged in writing to not take a job while in France. We’ve submitted passports, French identification cards, the lease multiple times, and proof of rent and utility payments. The latest query asks that the rent-payment format be un quittance de loyer, literally a rent demand, not a receipt. Our landlady got right on it, because even the French roll their eyes. The visa required a formal in-person interview to be booked no sooner than 60 days prior to visa expiration. I marked it on the calendar, but that changed. The Ministry’s latest initiative explains how to do-it-yourself sans interview along with new territory for us – geo-photos. Lest we forget, bureau was invented by the French. I wondered what inspires Americans to uproot their lives in the U.S. to make a home in Paris, so I asked some expat friends. Everyone knows that if you own a home in the U.S., you’ve got lots of stuff, entire rooms, closets, and garages full of belongings; and moving out of the country is a decision for strong shoulders and clear eyes. None of us underestimated the monumental task of a transcontinental move. Though the journey starts with one step, as ours did when Michael and I agreed to live in Paris, hundreds, if not thousands, of decisions followed, particularly, the nagging ones. Typically, people devoted two or more years to planning the move. One commonality is the will to make a sharp shift in one’s life. To travel more. To shake things up. To add a life challenge at retirement age. To keep brain cells alive. Those who moved to Paris while the children were still underfoot likely have a French spouse, which undoubtably paves the roadway to getting the notoriously tricky French driver’s license. Speaking French matters, Colorful beads form a cupola at the Metro entry for Palais Royal at Place Colette near Théatre de la Comédie Française. La Cupola at Galeries Lafayette. and when you’re a couple, you both possibly know some French. Michael and I both studied French in school; and by now, we’re reading French passably well. Our vocabulary continues to grow. but comprehension and conversational French will take more work. That we speak English to each other is a drawback. French is a challenge: I fault consonants that are silent at the beginning or the end of words; and vowels skipped in the middle of words, or clustered alarmingly, such as vieille or Montreuil. Remember memorization? Meet irregular verb tenses. Michael points out that French and Saxon birthed English, so therefore, English is based in French, except it’s not, as it’s more accurately based in Latin, and the French language is distinct from Italian. Yet didn’t the Duke of Normandy, William the Conqueror take the English throne in 1066? Saxon England, speaking German combined with French from the Normans, and the dual lingos are the basis for English. Voilà. Our Lake Merritt friends who have enjoyed decades in Paris are fluent in French. Boston friends who 10 years ago came to Paris to “stay a year,” and are still here, are disciplined students who practice French daily. Their go-to is Duolingo. pages.text: 26 Wednesday, February 9, 2022 AMERICANS IN PARIS By Patricia Forsyth Nº 48 in a biweekly series There’s no Welcome Wagon in France, commented my friend Ed recently. I was lamenting the myriad ways we’ve felt tripped up by French bureaucracy for the visa or healthcare and muttering about lost applications that had to be resubmitted resulting in duplicates and causing havoc. We’ve dutifully obtained translations into French of birth certificates, bank statements, and IRS 1040s. We’ve pledged in writing to not take a job while in France. We’ve submitted passports, French identification cards, the lease multiple times, and proof of rent and utility payments. The latest query asks that the rent-payment format be un quittance de loyer, literally a rent demand, not a receipt. Our landlady got right on it, because even the French roll their eyes. The visa required a formal in-person interview to be booked no sooner than 60 days prior to visa expiration. I marked it on the calendar, but that changed. The Ministry’s latest initiative explains how to do-it-yourself sans interview along with new Paris as an American Expat destination territory for us – geo-photos. Lest we forget, bureau was invented by the French. I wondered what inspires Americans to uproot their lives in the U.S. to make a home in Paris, so I asked some expat friends. Everyone knows that if you own a home in the U.S., you’ve got lots of stuff, entire rooms, closets, and garages full of belongings; and moving out of the country is a decision for strong shoulders and clear eyes. None of us underestimated the monumental task of a transcontinental move. Though the journey starts with one step, as ours did when Michael and I agreed to live in Paris, hundreds, if not thousands, of decisions followed, particularly, the nagging ones. Typically, people devoted two or more years to planning the move. One commonality is the will to make a sharp shift in one’s life. To travel more. To shake things up. To add a life challenge at retirement age. To keep brain cells alive. Those who moved to Paris while the children were still underfoot likely have a French spouse, which undoubtably paves the roadway to getting the notoriously tricky French driver’s license. Speaking French matters, Colorful beads form a cupola at the Metro entry for Palais Royal at Place Colette near Théatre de la Comédie Française. La Cupola at Galeries Lafayette. and when you’re a couple, you both possibly know some French. Michael and I both studied French in school; and by now, we’re reading French passably well. Our vocabulary continues to grow. but comprehension and conversational French will take more work. That we speak English to each other is a drawback. French is a challenge: I fault consonants that are silent at the beginning or the end of words; and vowels skipped in the middle of words, or clustered alarmingly, such as vieille or Montreuil. Remember memorization? Meet irregular verb tenses. Michael points out that French and Saxon birthed English, so therefore, English is based in French, except it’s not, as it’s more accurately based in Latin, and the French language is distinct from Italian. Yet didn’t the Duke of Normandy, William the Conqueror take the English throne in 1066? Saxon England, speaking German combined with French from the Normans, and the dual lingos are the basis for English. Voilà. Our Lake Merritt friends who have enjoyed decades in Paris are fluent in French. Boston friends who 10 years ago came to Paris to “stay a year,” and are still here, are disciplined students who practice French daily. Their go-to is Duolingo. articles.text: In the 1870s, Walter Blair was already a successful dairyman, quarryman and extensive land owner. Blair then turned his energy to transportation and developing horsecar lines. After partnering with investors to build a horsecar line from downtown Oakland to the end of Piedmont Avenue, Blair built his own line in 1878. The Ride to Blair’s Park Blair’s Piedmont Railway began where the Piedmont Avenue line ended and travelled from the gates of Mountain View Cemetery, through Blair’s grain fields, up to Vernal Avenue (now Highland Avenue) and on to the Piedmont Springs Hotel (currently Piedmont Park). Blair had the finest horsecar, with upholstered seats, a carpet on the floor and even a fringe on the top. He called it the “Palace Car.” It ran hourly and was the only public transportation to Piedmont. Newspapers of the day described a ride on Blair’s horsecar as a pleasant even romantic one, winding through fields of grain and up hillsides with birds singing, brooks murmuring, balmy air and gentle breezes. Blair’s Park To increase the number of passengers on his Piedmont Railway, Blair created Blair’s Park where families could escape the dusty streets of downtown Oakland and “spend a pleasant day rambling in the country.” He developed 40 acres of his own land between Mountain View Cemetery and Moraga Road as a picnic park. He began by thinning out some of the eucalyptus trees that grew as a border between his land and the cemetery’s. (Some of Blair’s original eucalyptus trees still grow along the cemetery border near the lakes.) Blair graded pathways and built several bridges over the stream that ran through his park. The paths led picnickers along the stream, through the ravine and up the hillsides among trees and wildflowers. He also constructed several dams and created small lakes. (The lakes in Mountain View Cemetery date back to Blair’s Park.) They said “Your stinking promises are making us stink with Pharoah. From this day forward keep that stinking talk of liberation to yourself.” Moses was left to cry to the Lord. “The overseers are calling the people lazy. The people are blaming me for their pain. I am blaming you for getting me in to this. Ever since we met at that bush, things have done nothing but go downhill. I don’t think you know what you are doing.” I don’t know all that Fannie Lou went through. Yet, almost certainly, she experienced personal attacks intended to undermine her work. She knew about the poor being blamed for their poverty. She knew about being accused of planting false hope. She knew about being reviled for putting burdens on the backs of the people instead of lifting them off. She knew about wanting to give up on God. In their approach to Pharoah, Moses and Aaron did not seek the freedom of their family and circle of friends alone. They sought the freedom of all the people. Yet, they knew that the people would not be free until they were free themselves. Fannie Lou Hamer shared their understanding. She courageously held on to it. She held onto it so courageously that Vice-President Kamala Harris quoted it in her 2020 speech to the Democratic National Convention as she accepted the nomination to be the Vice-Presidential candidate. Let us not turn our back on the stories of Moses, Aaron and Fannie Lou Hamer believing the lie that some us can be free while others toil in bondage. Freedom, as these heroes make clear, is a proposition of all of us or none. Jim Hopkins is Pastor of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, 3534 Lakeshore Avenue.in Oakland.
